title.en: Section 1 - A conversation about renting a flat
title.zh: 第一部分 - 关于租房的对话

sections.passage: A conversation between a letting agent, Anna, and a potential tenant, James, who is looking for a flat to rent in the city centre. James has recently accepted a job at a law firm and needs to move within the next two weeks. Anna describes three available properties. The first is a one-bedroom flat on Oak Street, located on the third floor of a modern apartment building. It has an open-plan kitchen and living area, a small balcony, and is fully furnished. The rent is 850 pounds per month, and the building has a secure entry system and a shared laundry room. The second property is a two-bedroom flat on Elm Road, on the ground floor of a converted Victorian house. It has a larger living space, a separate kitchen, and a small garden. The rent is 1,100 pounds per month, and it comes partially furnished. The third option is a studio apartment on Maple Lane, which is the most affordable at 650 pounds per month but is only 25 square metres and has no separate bedroom. James is most interested in the one-bedroom flat on Oak Street because it is close to his workplace and within his budget. Anna explains that the tenancy agreement is for a minimum of twelve months, with a security deposit of one month's rent required upfront. The tenant is responsible for paying council tax and utility bills, while the landlord covers building insurance and maintenance. James asks about the move-in date, and Anna says the flat will be available from the first of next month. He arranges to view the property the following afternoon at 2 PM.

title.en: Section 2 - A talk about a local museum
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于当地博物馆的介绍

sections.passage: A presentation by the director of the Riverside Museum, Dr. Peter Williams, about the museum's new exhibition and upcoming events. The museum, which was originally built in 1890 as a cotton mill, was converted into a museum in 1985 and now attracts approximately 250,000 visitors per year. Dr. Williams explains that the new temporary exhibition, which opens next month and runs for six months, is called 'Voices of the Industrial Revolution' and focuses on the experiences of ordinary workers during Britain's industrial transformation in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The exhibition features over 300 original artefacts, including tools, clothing, photographs, and personal letters, many of which have been donated by local families. A highlight of the exhibition is a recreated cotton mill workshop where visitors can experience the working conditions of the era, including the noise, heat, and long hours that factory workers endured. The museum has also developed an interactive digital experience using augmented reality technology, which allows visitors to see historical scenes overlaid on the current museum space through their smartphones. In addition to the exhibition, Dr. Williams describes the museum's programme of public events, including a series of evening lectures by academic historians, a children's workshop programme during school holidays, and a special heritage open day in October when admission will be free. He mentions that the museum recently received a grant of 500,000 pounds from the Heritage Lottery Fund, which will be used to renovate the ground floor galleries and improve accessibility for visitors with disabilities. The museum shop has been expanded and now stocks a wider range of books, locally made crafts, and educational materials.

title.en: Section 3 - A conversation about a science experiment
title.zh: 第三部分 - 关于科学实验的讨论

sections.passage: A conversation between two students, Mia and Lucas, who are planning an experiment for their Biology class. They need to investigate the effect of different light conditions on plant growth. They plan to use bean plants as their test subject because they grow quickly and are easy to measure. Their experiment will test four conditions: natural sunlight, artificial white light, red light only, and complete darkness. They will grow ten plants under each condition, using seeds from the same batch to ensure consistency. The experiment will run for four weeks, and they will measure the height of each plant and count the number of leaves every three days. Mia suggests using a light meter to record the exact intensity of light each plant receives, which will make their results more precise. Lucas agrees and also proposes recording the temperature and humidity in each growing environment, as these factors could affect the results. They need to control these variables to ensure a fair test. For watering, they decide to give each plant exactly 100 millilitres of water every two days. Their teacher, Ms. Roberts, has asked them to present their findings as a scientific report with the following sections: hypothesis, method, results, discussion, and conclusion. Lucas is concerned that four weeks might not be long enough to see significant differences, but Mia points out that previous studies have shown measurable differences in bean plant growth within two to three weeks under different light conditions. They also discuss potential sources of error, such as the fact that some seeds might be more viable than others, and they decide to start with 15 seeds per condition and remove the five weakest seedlings after the first week.

title.en: Section 4 - A lecture on the psychology of persuasion
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于说服心理学的讲座

sections.passage: A university lecture by Professor Robert Chen on the psychology of persuasion and its applications in marketing and public policy. Professor Chen begins by explaining that persuasion is one of the most studied topics in social psychology, and that researchers have identified six fundamental principles of influence. The first principle is reciprocity, which states that people feel obligated to return favours. Professor Chen gives the example of a study in which restaurant tips increased by 3 percent when customers were given a free mint with their bill. The second principle is commitment and consistency, which describes the tendency for people to behave consistently with their previous actions and statements. Once someone makes a small commitment, they are more likely to agree to a larger request. This technique, known as the foot-in-the-door method, has been shown to increase compliance rates by up to 50 percent in various studies. The third principle is social proof, which means that people are more likely to do something if they see others doing it. Hotels that display cards saying 'the majority of guests reuse their towels' see a significant increase in towel reuse compared to those that simply ask guests to be environmentally responsible. The fourth principle is authority, which demonstrates that people are more likely to follow the advice of perceived experts. This is why advertisements frequently feature doctors, scientists, or other authority figures. The fifth principle is liking, which shows that people are more easily persuaded by those they find attractive or similar to themselves. The sixth principle is scarcity, which suggests that people assign more value to things that are rare or becoming unavailable. Limited-time offers and exclusive deals exploit this psychological tendency. Professor Chen then discusses how these principles have been applied in public health campaigns, such as encouraging vaccination and promoting healthy eating, and in political campaigns to influence voter behaviour.

title.zh: 文章1 - 玻璃制造的历史

sections.passage: Glass is one of the oldest and most versatile materials known to humanity, with a history stretching back nearly 5,000 years. The earliest known glass objects were decorative beads, which were produced in Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3500 BC. These early glass items were made by coating a core of sand or clay with molten glass, and the technique was closely related to pottery glazing. The first true glass vessels appeared around 1500 BC in Egypt, where craftsmen developed a technique called core forming, in which molten glass was wound around a removable core to create small containers for perfumes and oils. The art of glassblowing, which revolutionised glass production, was invented in the Roman-controlled region of Syria around 50 BC. This technique involved inflating a blob of molten glass at the end of a blowpipe, which allowed craftsmen to create hollow vessels much more quickly and cheaply than previous methods. Glassblowing spread rapidly throughout the Roman Empire, and glass objects that had previously been luxury items available only to the wealthy became accessible to ordinary people. Roman glassmakers produced a wide variety of objects, including bottles, cups, bowls, and window glass. The Roman author Pliny the Elder attributed the discovery of glass to Phoenician sailors who, according to legend, accidentally created glass when they used blocks of natron, a natural soda compound, to support their cooking fire on a sandy beach. While this story is almost certainly a myth, it does highlight the essential raw materials of glassmaking: silica sand, soda ash, and limestone. During the medieval period, Venice became the centre of European glassmaking, and Venetian glassmakers, known as cristalleri, were renowned for their skill and artistry. In 1291, the Venetian government ordered all glassmakers to relocate to the island of Murano, ostensibly to reduce the risk of fire but also to help protect their trade secrets. Murano glassmakers developed numerous innovations, including cristallo, a remarkably clear glass that resembled rock crystal, and millefiori, a technique involving the fusion of coloured glass canes into intricate patterns.

title.zh: 文章2 - 双语能力的好处

sections.passage: For much of the twentieth century, researchers believed that bilingualism was a disadvantage for children's cognitive development. It was thought that trying to process two languages simultaneously placed excessive demands on the brain, leading to confusion, slower language development, and lower academic performance. However, research conducted over the past three decades has completely overturned this view, revealing that bilingualism confers a range of significant cognitive advantages. One of the most well-documented benefits is enhanced executive function. Executive function refers to a set of mental processes that include attention control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory. Studies have shown that bilingual individuals consistently outperform monolinguals on tasks that require the inhibition of distracting information, switching between different tasks, and holding multiple pieces of information in mind simultaneously. This advantage is believed to arise because bilinguals must constantly manage two active language systems, selecting the appropriate language for a given context while suppressing the other. This ongoing mental exercise strengthens the brain's executive control networks. Research has also shown that bilingualism may delay the onset of dementia. A landmark study conducted at the University of Toronto found that bilingual patients were diagnosed with dementia an average of 4.5 years later than monolingual patients, even when both groups showed equivalent levels of brain damage. This suggests that the cognitive reserve built up through years of managing two languages provides a buffer against age-related cognitive decline. Furthermore, bilingual individuals have been shown to have enhanced metalinguistic awareness, which is the ability to reflect on and manipulate language as a system. This heightened awareness can facilitate the learning of additional languages and improve overall literacy skills. Studies have also demonstrated that bilingual children develop better perspective-taking abilities, as managing two languages requires them to consider what their listener knows and which language is appropriate for a given situation. Despite these advantages, it is important to note that the degree of cognitive benefit depends on the level of bilingual proficiency and the frequency of language use. Passive knowledge of a second language is unlikely to produce the same cognitive advantages as active, regular use of both languages.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Ethics of Autonomous Vehicles
title.zh: 文章3 - 自动驾驶汽车的伦理

sections.passage: The development of autonomous vehicles promises to transform transportation, potentially reducing the approximately 1.35 million deaths that occur in road traffic accidents worldwide each year. However, the widespread adoption of self-driving cars raises profound ethical questions that go far beyond the technical challenges of engineering. The most prominent ethical dilemma facing autonomous vehicle developers is often called the trolley problem, a philosophical thought experiment that asks how an autonomous vehicle should respond when a collision is unavoidable. Should the vehicle be programmed to minimise total harm, even if that means sacrificing its passengers? Or should it prioritise the safety of its occupants at all costs? Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology created an online platform called the Moral Machine, which presented millions of people worldwide with scenarios involving autonomous vehicles and asked them to make difficult choices. The results revealed significant cultural differences in ethical preferences. For example, respondents from collectivist cultures, such as those in East Asia, were more likely to favour saving elderly people, while those from individualist cultures, such as the United States and Europe, tended to prefer saving younger people. These cultural variations make it extremely difficult to create a universal ethical framework for autonomous vehicles. Beyond the trolley problem, there are numerous other ethical considerations. Questions of legal liability arise when autonomous vehicles are involved in accidents. Who is responsible: the manufacturer, the software developer, the vehicle owner, or the occupant? Current legal frameworks are not equipped to handle these questions, and lawmakers in many countries are struggling to develop appropriate regulations. Privacy is another major concern, as autonomous vehicles generate vast amounts of data about their passengers' movements, habits, and destinations. There are also concerns about the potential for surveillance and the risk that this data could be hacked or misused. The impact on employment must also be considered, as the automation of driving could displace millions of professional drivers worldwide, including taxi drivers, truck drivers, and delivery workers. Some experts predict that up to 5 million driving jobs could be lost in the United States alone within the next two decades.

text.zh: 美国在二十年内可能失去多少驾驶工作岗位？

text.en: What is the trolley problem about?
text.zh: 电车难题是关于什么的？

options.en: How a vehicle should respond when a collision is unavoidable
options.zh: 当碰撞不可避免时车辆应如何应对

options.en: How to program vehicles to follow traffic laws
options.zh: 如何编程车辆遵守交通法规

options.en: How to make vehicles more fuel efficient

text.en: What did individualist culture respondents tend to prefer?
text.zh: 个人主义文化受访者倾向于偏好什么？

options.zh: 数据被黑客攻击或滥用

Because of cultural variations in ethical preferences

因为汽车公司意见不一

prompt.en: The charts below show the results of a survey conducted to find out what people in different age groups thought were the most important things in life. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh: 下面的图表展示了一项调查的结果，旨在了解不同年龄段的人认为生活中最重要的事情是什么。通过选择和报告主要特征来总结信息，并在相关之处进行比较。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en: Some people think that instead of preventing climate change, we need to find a way to live with it. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些人认为，与其阻止气候变化，我们需要找到一种与之共存的方式。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？给出你的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中的任何相关例子。至少写250个单词。
